records.name: Circle of Competence

origin.author: Warren Buffett
origin.work: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Know the areas where your judgment has a track record and where it does not. Inside them, act; outside them, slow down, borrow expertise or stay out.
records.key_question: Is this inside my circle, and what is the evidence that it is?
use_when: high confidence with thin track record
evaluating advice from outside the speaker's field
records.produces: explicit in/out boundary plus who to consult outside it
records.failure_mode: Used as permanent justification for never entering a new domain.

records.name: Second-Order Thinking

origin.author: Howard Marks
origin.work: The Most Important Thing
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Look past the immediate result to the reactions it triggers: who responds, how, and what follows from their response. First effects are often the opposite of later ones.
records.key_question: Who reacts to this, and what happens after their reaction?
records.produces: consequence chain with named reacting actors
records.failure_mode: Speculative chains presented as forecast; infinite regress used to avoid deciding.

records.name: Inversion

origin.author: Carl Jacobi
origin.work: Jacobi's maxim, popularised by Charlie Munger
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Approach the problem backwards: ask what would make it fail, or what you want to avoid, then steer away from that. Often clearer than asking directly how to succeed.
records.key_question: What would guarantee failure here, and am I doing any of it?
records.produces: ranked avoid-list of failure paths
records.failure_mode: Avoidance-only strategy that eliminates downside without ever building upside.

records.name: Occam's Razor

origin.author: William of Ockham
origin.work: Principle of parsimony
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Between explanations that fit the facts equally well, start with the one that needs the fewest extra assumptions. A default for ordering hypotheses, not proof that the simple one is right.
records.key_question: Which explanation requires the fewest unsupported assumptions?
records.produces: explanations ranked by assumption load
records.failure_mode: Amputating real complexity. Simplicity is a tiebreaker, not evidence of truth.

records.name: Hanlon's Razor

origin.author: Robert J. Hanlon
origin.work: Murphy's Law Book Two (Arthur Bloch)
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Before concluding someone acted out of malice, check whether carelessness, ignorance or confusion would explain it. Those are far more common causes of harm.
records.key_question: Do incompetence, constraint or incentive explain this before malice does?
records.produces: alternative causal candidates ranked by prior likelihood
records.failure_mode: Excusing repeated, patterned harm that has already outrun the incompetence explanation.

records.name: Relativity

origin.author: Albert Einstein
origin.work: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: What you see depends on where you stand. Your position, history and interests shape what looks obvious, so ask how the situation appears from other positions before judging it.
records.key_question: From whose vantage point is this behaviour rational?
records.produces: frame inventory: what each actor sees, values and cannot see
records.failure_mode: Sliding from relativity of perception into relativism about validity.

records.name: Self-Preservation
records.evidence_note: Self-protective motives are well supported across species; terror-management studies on the human side have mixed replication. Treat as a motive to expect, not a predictor of any act.

origin.author: Richard Dawkins
origin.work: The Selfish Gene
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: People and organisations act to protect their own survival, status and position. Expect this drive to shape behaviour, especially when change threatens someone.
records.key_question: Whose identity, status or security is threatened by this?
records.produces: threat map by actor
records.failure_mode: Psychologising a substantive disagreement into a threat response.

records.name: Sampling

origin.author: Jacob Bernoulli
origin.work: Ars Conjectandi (law of large numbers)
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Conclusions are only as good as the sample behind them. Small or unrepresentative samples mislead, so ask how the data was gathered and how much of it there is.
records.key_question: How many observations is this built on, and how were they selected?
records.produces: sample adequacy verdict and selection bias check
records.failure_mode: Demanding impossible sample sizes as a device for stalling decisions.

records.name: Randomness

origin.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
origin.work: Fooled by Randomness
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Many outcomes contain a large element of chance. Allow for luck when explaining results, and avoid reading patterns into noise.
records.key_question: Could this outcome be noise?
records.produces: noise-versus-signal verdict
records.failure_mode: Attributing everything to luck, which dissolves accountability entirely.

records.name: Regression to the Mean

origin.author: Francis Galton
origin.work: Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: An extreme result is usually followed by one closer to average, because chance contributed to the extreme. Do not credit or blame an intervention for that return.
records.key_question: Was this extreme, and what is the expected next value without any intervention?
use_when: after a record quarter or a disaster
records.produces: adjusted expectation and counterfactual baseline
records.failure_mode: Calling a genuine trend regression to the mean.

records.name: Bubbles
records.evidence_note: Historical bubbles are well catalogued (Kindleberger); experimental bubbles replicate (Smith, Suchanek and Williams 1988). Spotting a bubble in real time is not reliable.

origin.author: Charles Kindleberger
origin.work: Manias, Panics and Crashes
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Prices or enthusiasm can rise far beyond underlying value when people buy because others are buying. Bubbles are easy to see in hindsight and hard to time from inside.
records.key_question: Is enthusiasm detached from fundamentals, and what story is sustaining it?
use_when: fear of missing out on an asset or trend
records.produces: gap between fundamentals and narrative
records.failure_mode: Calling every rise a bubble and missing a genuine regime change.

records.name: Framing
records.evidence_note: Framing effects (Tversky and Kahneman 1981) replicate broadly, with size varying by task and population.

origin.author: Amos Tversky; Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: How a choice is presented changes how people respond to it, even when the facts are the same. Check whether you would decide differently under another framing.
records.key_question: How does the presentation change the response, and who chose that frame?
records.produces: the operative frame plus two alternative framings
records.failure_mode: Reframing used as a substitute for changing substance, which is manipulation.

records.name: Representation

origin.author: Charles Sanders Peirce
origin.work: Semiotics (sign, object, interpretant)
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A representation stands in for something else and always selects and distorts. Ask what a chart, symbol or summary leaves out before trusting it.
records.key_question: What does this metric, word or model hide, and whose interpretation does it encode?
records.produces: distortion inventory of the representation
records.failure_mode: Endless critique of representations with no working substitute offered.

records.name: Bias from Incentives
records.evidence_note: Self-serving bias in judgment is replicated (auditor and expert-advice studies, e.g. Moore and Loewenstein). Awareness alone does not remove it.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.work: The Psychology of Human Misjudgment
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: People sincerely come to believe what it pays them to believe. When judging a claim, ask what the source gains if you accept it.
records.key_question: What does the person telling me this get if I believe it?
records.produces: claims re-weighted by the incentive behind them
records.failure_mode: Dismissing every interested party, when the most informed people are usually interested.

records.name: Pavlovian Association
records.evidence_note: Classical conditioning is among the most replicated findings in psychology (Pavlov 1927). Human consumer-association effects are smaller and less consistent.

origin.author: Ivan Pavlov
origin.work: Conditioned Reflexes
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Repeated pairing of a stimulus with an experience makes the stimulus trigger the response on its own. Many reactions are learned associations, not judgments.
records.key_question: What associations attach to this beyond its substance?
use_when: aversion to a task or meeting
records.produces: association inventory, positive and negative
records.failure_mode: Engineering associations as a replacement for improving the underlying thing.

records.name: Envy and Jealousy
records.evidence_note: Social comparison and envy-driven behaviour appear in experiments (costly punishment and spite in economic games). Strength varies by culture and individual.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.work: The Psychology of Human Misjudgment
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: People compare their position with others and resent those who have more. Envy and jealousy drive choices that make no sense on absolute terms.
records.key_question: Who is comparing themselves to whom, and what does that comparison cost?
records.produces: relative-position map
records.failure_mode: Reducing a legitimate fairness claim to envy in order to dismiss it.

records.name: Liking/Loving and Disliking/Hating
records.evidence_note: Liking colours judgment: halo effect (Thorndike 1920; Nisbett and Wilson 1977) and similarity-liking findings. Effect sizes vary.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.work: The Psychology of Human Misjudgment
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We overrate people and things we like and underrate those we dislike, including the evidence they bring. Separate the messenger from the message.
records.key_question: Would I reach this judgement if someone I dislike had said it?
records.produces: source-blind re-evaluation
records.failure_mode: Overcorrecting against people you like, which is the same error signed differently.

records.name: Denial
records.evidence_note: Defensive avoidance of threatening information is documented (ostrich effect; motivated reasoning, Kunda 1990). Individual variation is large; denial as a mechanism is hard to test.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.work: The Psychology of Human Misjudgment
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: When a truth is painful, people avoid seeing it. Denial protects comfort in the short term and lets problems grow in the long term.
records.key_question: What evidence am I declining to look at, and why that one?
records.produces: explicit list of evidence being avoided
records.failure_mode: 'You're in denial' used as an unfalsifiable debate move against others.

records.name: Availability Heuristic
records.evidence_note: Tversky and Kahneman (1973) showed judged frequency tracks ease of recall. Later work refines the mechanism (ease versus content); the core effect replicates.

origin.author: Amos Tversky; Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Recent, vivid or frequent events feel more probable than they are.
records.key_question: Is this vivid because it is frequent, or frequent-seeming because it is vivid?
records.produces: frequency correction against actual data
records.failure_mode: Dismissing recent evidence precisely because it is recent.

records.name: Failure to Account for Base Rates

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman; Amos Tversky
origin.work: On the Psychology of Prediction
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Before judging a specific case, start from how often outcomes like it happen in general. Vivid details tempt us to ignore those background frequencies.
records.key_question: What is the historical frequency for cases like this, before I look at this case's specifics?
records.produces: reference class and the prior it implies
records.failure_mode: Choosing the reference class that produces the conclusion you wanted.

records.name: Tendency to Stereotype
records.evidence_note: Categorical judgment is documented in social cognition. Accuracy of stereotypes is a disputed research area (Jussim); use as a warning about shortcuts, not a verdict on any group.

origin.author: Walter Lippmann
origin.work: Public Opinion
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Sorting people and things into categories saves effort but erases individual differences. Check whether the category actually predicts anything about this case.
records.key_question: Am I using a category where individuating evidence is actually available?
records.produces: specificity check: what individuating data exists
records.failure_mode: Refusing all categorisation, which discards genuine base-rate information.

records.name: Failure to See False Conjunctions

origin.author: Amos Tversky; Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: Extensional versus Intuitive Reasoning
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A detailed scenario can feel more likely than a broader one that contains it, though it cannot be. Each added detail lowers the probability.
records.key_question: Am I rating a detailed scenario as more likely than the broader case that contains it?
records.produces: probability correction toward the parent category
records.failure_mode: Rejecting useful specificity in planning because it is technically less probable.

records.name: Social Proof
records.evidence_note: Conformity (Asch 1951) and informational social influence replicate, with size varying by culture, group size and task.

origin.author: Robert Cialdini
origin.work: Influence
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We take others' behaviour as evidence of what is right, especially when unsure. Check whether the crowd has independent evidence or is copying itself.
records.key_question: Am I believing this because of evidence, or because of who else believes it?
records.produces: independent evidence check separate from consensus
records.failure_mode: Contrarianism as identity: rejecting consensus because it is consensus.

records.name: Narrative Instinct
records.evidence_note: Narrative fallacy is argued by Taleb from cases; related support exists in explanation-seeking studies. Direct tests of the claimed bias are limited.

origin.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
origin.work: The Black Swan
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We understand events as stories with causes, characters and meaning. Stories are memorable and persuasive, which makes them easy to accept without checking.
records.key_question: Is this a story fitted to a known outcome, or an explanation that would have predicted it?
records.produces: separation of narrative from predictive evidence
records.failure_mode: Rejecting narrative entirely; it remains how humans are actually persuaded.

records.name: First-Conclusion Bias
records.evidence_note: Anchoring and early-hypothesis lock-in are documented (Tversky and Kahneman 1974; primacy in diagnostic reasoning). Sizes vary and expertise reduces some of it.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.work: The Psychology of Human Misjudgment
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: The first plausible explanation tends to stop the search for others. Treat the first conclusion as one candidate and deliberately generate alternatives.
records.key_question: What are my second and third hypotheses?
records.produces: at least two rival hypotheses with discriminating tests
records.failure_mode: Endless option generation that prevents any decision being made.

records.name: Overgeneralization from Small Samples

origin.author: Amos Tversky; Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: Belief in the Law of Small Numbers
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A few cases can look like a rule. Small samples swing widely by chance, so gather more instances before generalising.
records.key_question: How many cases is this rule built on, and where does it stop applying?
records.produces: scope limit on the claim
records.failure_mode: Refusing to act until n is large, in domains where n is never large.

records.name: Relative Satisfaction/Misery
records.evidence_note: Income comparison affects reported well-being (Easterlin 1974; Luttmer 2005). Whether absolute income also matters is disputed (Stevenson and Wolfers 2008).

origin.author: Richard Easterlin
origin.work: Does Economic Growth Improve the Human Lot?
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Satisfaction depends on comparison with expectations, past experience and other people more than on absolute conditions. A better situation can feel worse.
records.key_question: Compared to what, and who chose that comparison?
records.produces: named comparison set and its alternatives
records.failure_mode: Dismissing real problems as 'merely relative'.

records.name: Commitment and Consistency Bias
records.evidence_note: Cognitive dissonance findings (Festinger 1957) and foot-in-the-door effects are documented; several classic paradigms replicate with smaller effects than first reported.

origin.author: Leon Festinger
origin.work: A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Once people commit, publicly or privately, they tend to act consistently with it even when evidence changes. Revisit commitments as if making them fresh.
records.key_question: Am I holding this because it is right, or because I already said it?
records.produces: reassessment made independent of prior commitment
records.failure_mode: Abandoning commitments the moment they become costly, which destroys trust.

records.name: Hindsight Bias
records.evidence_note: Fischhoff (1975) found outcome knowledge inflates 'I knew it' judgments. It replicates widely and is hard to remove.

origin.author: Baruch Fischhoff
origin.work: Hindsight is not equal to foresight
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Once the outcome is known, it seems to have been predictable all along. Record your expectations beforehand so you can judge decisions on what was knowable.
records.key_question: What did I actually record before the outcome was known?
records.produces: comparison against a decision log
records.failure_mode: Refusing to learn from outcomes at all on the grounds that hindsight is unreliable.

records.name: Sensitivity to Fairness
records.evidence_note: Ultimatum-game rejections of unfair offers (Güth 1982) replicate across many societies; the threshold varies by culture.

origin.author: Werner Güth; Rolf Schmittberger; Bernd Schwarze
origin.work: An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: People react strongly to treatment they see as unfair, even at a cost to themselves. Systems that feel unfair invite resistance however efficient they are.
records.key_question: Will this be experienced as fair, and by whose standard?
records.produces: fairness impact assessment per affected group
records.failure_mode: Fairness optics substituted for fair outcomes, which is detected and punished.

records.name: Overestimate Consistency of Behavior
records.evidence_note: Correspondence bias (Jones and Harris 1967; Ross 1977) replicates; strength differs across cultures. Behaviour has stable and situational components.

origin.author: Lee Ross
origin.work: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We attribute others' behaviour to their personality and underweight the situation they were in. The same person can act very differently in different contexts.
records.key_question: Trait or situation: what would I conclude if I could only see the context?
records.produces: situational alternative explanation alongside the trait one
records.failure_mode: Excusing repeated behaviour as situational when the pattern is the evidence.

records.name: Influence of Stress
records.evidence_note: Acute stress impairs prefrontal function and shifts people toward habit in laboratory studies (Arnsten 2009; Schwabe and Wolf). Evidence is mostly acute-stress lab work.

origin.author: Amy Arnsten
origin.work: Stress signalling pathways that impair prefrontal cortex structure and function
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Under stress, people fall back on habits and quick reactions and are more open to bias. Expect worse judgment in a crisis and set up decisions in advance.
records.key_question: What state am I deciding from, and what does that state degrade?
records.produces: state check plus deferral rule for reversible decisions
records.failure_mode: Using stress as grounds to dismiss a sound decision that was made under pressure.

records.name: Survivorship Bias

origin.author: Abraham Wald
origin.work: Statistical Research Group memoranda on aircraft survivability
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We see the cases that survived and miss those that failed, so lessons drawn from survivors alone can be wrong. Look for the missing failures before drawing conclusions.
records.key_question: Where are the ones who did the same thing and failed?
records.produces: missing-losers analysis and what it does to the inference
records.failure_mode: Dismissing all learning from winners; some winners did have a real edge.

records.name: Tendency to Want to Do Something
records.evidence_note: Penalty-kick goalkeepers dive more often than staying put would justify (Bar-Eli et al. 2007). Generalisation to other domains rests on fewer studies.

origin.author: Michael Bar-Eli et al.
origin.work: Action bias among elite soccer goalkeepers
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: There is a strong pull to act, especially when watched or under pressure, even when waiting would be better. Ask whether action improves the outcome or only relieves discomfort.
records.key_question: Is action required, or am I acting to feel useful?
records.produces: do-nothing option explicitly costed alongside the others
records.failure_mode: Inaction rationalised as discipline when the cost of waiting is the larger risk.

records.name: Confirmation Bias and Falsification

origin.author: Karl Popper; Peter Wason
origin.work: The Logic of Scientific Discovery; On the failure to eliminate hypotheses
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We notice and seek evidence that supports what we already think. Counter it by stating what would show you wrong and looking for that evidence first.
records.key_question: What evidence would change my mind, and have I gone looking for it?
records.produces: explicit falsification test and where to run it
records.failure_mode: Demanding falsifiability of questions that are not empirical.

records.name: Myside Bias

origin.author: Keith E. Stanovich, Richard F. West & Maggie E. Toplak
origin.work: Myside Bias, Rational Thinking, and Intelligence (Current Directions in Psychological Science)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Keith E. Stanovich, Richard F. West & Maggie E. Toplak, 2013); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: People evaluate evidence, generate arguments and test hypotheses asymmetrically in favour of their own prior position — and, uniquely among biases, intelligence does not protect against it.
records.key_question: Would we find this evidence convincing if it supported the other side — and are we applying the same standard of proof to both?
use_when: an argument, analysis or recommendation produced by someone with a known
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Because it is uncorrelated with ability, smart teams dismiss the audit as applying only to other people — which is the bias operating.

records.name: Motivated Reasoning

origin.author: Ziva Kunda
origin.work: The Case for Motivated Reasoning (Psychological Bulletin)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Ziva Kunda, 1990); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Reasoning is steered by the conclusion the reasoner wants to reach: congenial evidence is waved through, uncongenial evidence is cross-examined.
records.key_question: What conclusion does the author of this argument need to be true — and does the rigour of their scrutiny change exactly where that need changes?
use_when: a justification, business case or defence written by the person who
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: The audit can itself be motivated — it is easy to diagnose motivated reasoning only in opponents, so it must be run on one's own side first.

records.name: Identity-Protective Cognition

origin.author: Dan M. Kahan, Donald Braman, John Gastil, Paul Slovic & C. K. Mertz
origin.work: Culture and Identity-Protective Cognition: Explaining the White-Male Effect in Risk Perception (Journal of Empirical Legal Studies)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Dan M. Kahan, Donald Braman, John Gastil, Paul Slovic & C. K. Mertz, 2007); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: People credit or dismiss evidence to protect their standing in a group they belong to, so on identity-loaded questions more information and more ability often deepen the split instead of closing it.
records.key_question: What would it cost the person socially — with their own side — to accept this evidence, and is that cost doing the evaluating?
use_when: a claim or plan entangled with politics, culture, profession or tribe
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Treating the disagreement as an information deficit and piling on more data, which gives identity more material to work against.

records.name: Bias Blind Spot

origin.author: Emily Pronin, Daniel Y. Lin & Lee Ross
origin.work: The Bias Blind Spot: Perceptions of Bias in Self Versus Others (Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Emily Pronin, Daniel Y. Lin & Lee Ross, 2002); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: People readily detect bias in others while rating themselves largely immune, because they check their own thinking by introspection and others' by behaviour.
records.key_question: This audit found biases in everyone else's judgment — what evidence do we have that the same checks pass on ours?
use_when: the red team itself, and any reviewer, approver or expert panel delivering
run the bias blind spot test
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It cannot be removed by awareness; naming it in the room produces agreement that it applies to the room in general and no one in particular.

records.name: Groupthink

origin.author: Irving L. Janis
origin.work: Victims of Groupthink

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Irving L. Janis, 1972); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: A cohesive group under a directive leader suppresses dissent, self-censors and manufactures unanimity, producing decisions no member would have defended alone.
records.key_question: When did anyone in this group last disagree out loud — and what happened to them when they did?
use_when: a unanimous plan or verdict from a tight-knit team, especially under time
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Unanimity is taken as evidence of correctness, when in this failure mode it is the symptom to be explained.

records.name: Abilene Paradox

origin.author: Jerry B. Harvey
origin.work: The Abilene Paradox: The Management of Agreement (Organizational Dynamics)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Jerry B. Harvey, 1974); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: A group collectively decides on a course of action that most or all members privately oppose, because each wrongly assumes the others support it and stays silent.
records.key_question: If every person in this room voted anonymously right now, would this plan still pass?
use_when: a consensus decision that nobody seems enthusiastic about and nobody can
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Unlike groupthink there is no pressure or illusion of invulnerability — just unspoken private disagreement — so exhortations to 'be bold' miss the mechanism entirely.

records.name: Pluralistic Ignorance

origin.author: Daniel Katz, Floyd H. Allport & Margaret B. Jenness
origin.work: Students' Attitudes: A Report of the Syracuse University Research Study

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Daniel Katz, Floyd H. Allport & Margaret B. Jenness, 1931); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Most members of a group privately reject a norm or claim but publicly conform, because each misreads everyone else's conformity as genuine agreement.
records.key_question: Are we measuring what people here actually believe, or what each of them believes the rest believe?
use_when: survey results, meeting assent, market 'consensus' or cultural claims cited
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Public signals are treated as private conviction, so the false consensus survives every poll that asks people to speak in front of each other.

records.name: Anchoring

origin.author: Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Science)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, 1974); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Numerical judgments are pulled toward the first number on the table — even an arbitrary or admitted-irrelevant one — and adjust away from it insufficiently.
records.key_question: Where did the first number in this discussion come from, and how far would the estimate move if it had never been said?
use_when: any estimate, price, budget, timeline or target that was negotiated or
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Expertise and warnings barely weaken it; the anchor works even when everyone in the room can name the bias.

records.name: Attribute Substitution

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman & Shane Frederick
origin.work: Representativeness Revisited: Attribute Substitution in Intuitive Judgment (in Heuristics and Biases)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Daniel Kahneman & Shane Frederick, 2002); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Faced with a hard target question, the mind silently answers an easier related one — liking for quality, fluency for truth, similarity for probability — and reports that answer instead.
records.key_question: What question was actually asked, and what easier question did this judgment answer in its place?
use_when: a verdict on quality, risk, likelihood or value that arrived quickly and
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: The substitution is invisible to the judge because the easy answer arrives with the confidence of the hard one.

records.name: WYSIATI (What You See Is All There Is)

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: Thinking, Fast and Slow

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Daniel Kahneman, 2011); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Judgment builds the most coherent story possible from the evidence currently visible and does not spontaneously ask what evidence is missing.
records.key_question: What is not in this picture at all — which facts, if they existed, would change the story, and did anyone go looking for them?
use_when: a confident narrative, diagnosis or recommendation built from a single
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Adding more of the same kind of evidence strengthens the story's coherence without strengthening its truth.

records.name: Planning Fallacy

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky
origin.work: Intuitive Prediction: Biases and Corrective Procedures

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky, 1979); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Plans forecast the best case: timelines and budgets are built from the inside view of this project and systematically ignore how similar projects actually went.
records.key_question: This schedule assumes nearly everything goes right — what did the same people's last three estimates look like against what happened?
use_when: a project plan, launch date, budget or roadmap presented as a single
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Padding is added performatively and then negotiated away, because the base estimate was never anchored to an outcome distribution.

records.name: Overconfidence

origin.author: Baruch Fischhoff, Paul Slovic & Sarah Lichtenstein
origin.work: Knowing with Certainty: The Appropriateness of Extreme Confidence (Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Baruch Fischhoff, Paul Slovic & Sarah Lichtenstein, 1977); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Stated confidence systematically exceeds accuracy — events claimed to be certain fail at rates no one in the room would accept if they were stated as odds.
records.key_question: If this 'certain' claim were priced as a bet, what odds would the person actually accept — and how often have their past certainties been wrong?
use_when: a claim, forecast or expert verdict delivered with high or total confidence.
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Confidence is read socially as competence, so the most overconfident voice in the room gains influence precisely where it should lose it.

records.name: Affect Heuristic

origin.author: Melissa L. Finucane, Ali Alhakami, Paul Slovic & Stephen M. Johnson
origin.work: The Affect Heuristic in Judgments of Risks and Benefits (Journal of Behavioral Decision Making)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Melissa L. Finucane, Ali Alhakami, Paul Slovic & Stephen M. Johnson, 2000); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Risk and benefit are read off one feeling: liked things are judged low-risk and high-benefit, disliked things the reverse, although in reality risk and benefit usually rise together.
records.key_question: Are the risk and benefit estimates in this case suspiciously opposite — and would either survive being assessed by someone indifferent to the proposal?
use_when: a risk assessment or pitch where the same team scored both the dangers and
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Information about benefit alone moves the risk judgment, so a better pitch silently rewrites the risk register.

records.name: Scope Insensitivity

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman & Jack L. Knetsch
origin.work: Valuing Public Goods: The Purchase of Moral Satisfaction (Journal of Environmental Economics and Management)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Daniel Kahneman & Jack L. Knetsch, 1992); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Judgments of quantity barely respond to quantity: people offer nearly the same response for saving 2,000, 20,000 or 200,000 of something, because they are picturing a prototype, not a number.
records.key_question: If this problem were ten times larger or smaller, would the proposed response change at all — and if not, what is it responding to?
use_when: a valuation, impact claim, market sizing or harm estimate driven by a vivid
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: The prototype image does the work, so multiplying the real scope multiplies nothing in the judgment.

records.name: Focusing Illusion

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman, Alan B. Krueger, David Schkade, Norbert Schwarz & Arthur A. Stone
origin.work: Would You Be Happier If You Were Richer? A Focusing Illusion (Science)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Daniel Kahneman, Alan B. Krueger, David Schkade, Norbert Schwarz & Arthur A. Stone, 2006); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it: whatever the judgment focuses on gets its weight inflated.
records.key_question: This factor dominates the analysis because it is the topic — how much of the outcome does it actually explain across a whole day, year or budget?
use_when: a decision hinging on one salient attribute — salary, one feature, one
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: The audit itself focuses attention, so the check must compare against the full set of factors, not just argue the salient one down.

records.name: Sunk Cost

origin.author: Hal R. Arkes & Catherine Blumer
origin.work: The Psychology of Sunk Cost (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Hal R. Arkes & Catherine Blumer, 1985); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Money, time and effort already spent — which no decision can recover — keep pulling investment into failing courses of action to avoid admitting the loss.
records.key_question: If we arrived today with nothing spent, would we fund this at its remaining cost for its remaining expected value?
use_when: a continuation, renewal or 'one more push' decision on a project with a
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Each new tranche is justified by the last, so the total committed grows past any point at which a fresh decision-maker would have entered.

records.name: Status Quo Bias

origin.author: William Samuelson & Richard Zeckhauser
origin.work: Status Quo Bias in Decision Making (Journal of Risk and Uncertainty)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (William Samuelson & Richard Zeckhauser, 1988); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Options are preferred because they are the current arrangement, beyond what their merits justify — the default wins by being the default.
records.key_question: If the alternative were the status quo and our current arrangement were the proposal, would we vote to switch to it?
use_when: a renewal, an incumbent vendor, an existing policy or any 'why change?'
run the status quo bias test
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It compounds with sunk cost and omission bias until the burden of proof on change becomes impossible to meet.

records.name: Authority Bias

origin.author: Stanley Milgram
origin.work: Behavioral Study of Obedience (Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Stanley Milgram, 1963); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Claims gain credence from the rank, title or confidence of the person stating them, independently of the evidence offered.
records.key_question: Would this claim survive if it were read aloud unattributed — and has anyone checked the evidence rather than the CV?
use_when: an expert endorsement, a senior sponsor's assertion, or a famous name used
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: Deference is socially rewarded and dissent is costly, so the audit has to be procedural (blind the source) rather than exhortatory.

records.name: Halo Effect

origin.author: Edward L. Thorndike
origin.work: A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings (Journal of Applied Psychology)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Edward L. Thorndike, 1920); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: One salient trait — success, attractiveness, a famous employer — bleeds into ratings of every other trait, so independent qualities are scored as if they were one.
records.key_question: Are these separate scores actually separate evidence, or one strong impression wearing several hats?
use_when: a judgment about a person, company or product where one standout feature is
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It survives explicit instruction to rate independently; only genuinely separate evidence per dimension breaks it (see MAP).

records.name: Fundamental Attribution Error

origin.author: Lee Ross
origin.work: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings (Advances in Experimental Social Psychology)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Lee Ross, 1977); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Others' behaviour is explained by their character while the pressures of their situation are discounted — so failures get blamed on people that a different person in the same seat would also have produced.
records.key_question: What would have to be true about the situation for a competent, well-intentioned person to have done exactly this?

run the fundamental attribution error test
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It is the default setting of post-mortems, so situational causes are only found when the audit forces them to be listed first.

records.name: Self-Serving Bias

origin.author: Dale T. Miller & Michael Ross
origin.work: Self-Serving Biases in the Attribution of Causality: Fact or Fiction? (Psychological Bulletin)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Dale T. Miller & Michael Ross, 1975); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Success is attributed to one's own skill and failure to circumstances — in oneself and one's team — corrupting every lessons-learned exercise built on self-report.
records.key_question: In this account, who gets credit for the wins and what gets blamed for the losses — and would the pattern reverse if the outcomes did?
use_when: a self-assessment, post-mortem, case study or track record presented by its
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: The account is usually sincere, which makes it persuasive; only contemporaneous records (decision journals) can correct it.

records.name: Negativity Bias

origin.author: Roy F. Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer & Kathleen D. Vohs
origin.work: Bad Is Stronger Than Good (Review of General Psychology)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Roy F. Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer & Kathleen D. Vohs, 2001); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: Bad events, bad feedback and bad possibilities weigh more than equivalent good ones, so a single vivid downside can veto a favourable balance of evidence.
records.key_question: Is the negative case weighted because it is more probable, or because it is more negative — and what does the symmetric upside look like?
use_when: a risk review, rejection or go/no-go where one bad scenario dominates a
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It masquerades as prudence, so challenging it reads as recklessness unless the audit compares like with like numerically.

records.name: Optimism Bias

origin.author: Tali Sharot
origin.work: The Optimism Bias

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Tali Sharot, 2011); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: People systematically overestimate the likelihood of good outcomes for themselves specifically — their project, their health, their venture — while rating others' chances more soberly.
records.key_question: Are these odds the ones the person would assign to a stranger attempting the identical thing?
use_when: a founder's, patient's or sponsor's estimate of their own prospects.
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It is selective — the same person can be pessimistic about the world and optimistic about themselves — so generic risk warnings slide off.

records.name: Dunning–Kruger Effect

origin.author: Justin Kruger & David Dunning
origin.work: Unskilled and Unaware of It (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Justin Kruger & David Dunning, 1999); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: The skills needed to produce a correct answer are the same skills needed to recognise one, so the least competent judges are the most confident that they are competent.
records.key_question: What test, independent of the person's own assessment, establishes that this judge can actually tell good work from bad in this domain?
use_when: a confident verdict from someone whose expertise in the specific domain is
records.produces: a named discount: the direction of the distortion and the adjustment it demands
records.failure_mode: It cannot be self-diagnosed — asking the person to reflect harder uses the very capacity that is missing — so the audit must be an external performance check.
